● In Canada, where the 0.5 mg Emerade device is available, the manufacturer suggests using this for adults >60 kg, and a Canadian position statement suggested this be prescribed for those weighing 45 kg (99 lb) or more [36].
KEY TEACHING POINTS

There are several important teaching points that should be emphasized when instructing patients in optimal use of epinephrine autoinjectors. These should be reviewed with patients at regular intervals. Patient information that reiterates these teaching points is also available. (See 'Information for patients' below.)
Anaphylaxis is unpredictable

Patients should understand that anaphylaxis is highly unpredictable [37]. One exposure to an allergen may result in mild symptoms while the next causes a life-threatening reaction or vice versa for reasons that are not fully understood.
Epinephrine is the best treatment available

The patient should be assured that epinephrine is the most effective treatment available for anaphylaxis and that having self-administered epinephrine available will enable the patient to start treatment without delay [3]. Fatal anaphylaxis is associated with lack of availability of epinephrine or failure to administer epinephrine promptly [38-40]. This fact may be expressed to the patient as the following: "In most cases of anaphylaxis that prove fatal, the person who died either did not have epinephrine available or had it available but did not use it. Thus, by having epinephrine and knowing how to use it, the patient already has a significant advantage."
Carry epinephrine at all times

Epinephrine autoinjectors or nasal sprays must be carried at all times in order to be available when the drug is actually needed. Patients may make the mistake of having their epinephrine on hand only in the setting where they spend most time (ie, home, school, or work). However, they may be at particular risk for anaphylaxis when out of their normal routines (eg, during exercise, while dining out, attending celebrations and banquets, or traveling). Thus, patients should devise a way for epinephrine to be available at all times. This may mean storing devices in multiple locations or carrying a small bag containing the device and other essential items that is taken everywhere, without exception.
Antihistamines or asthma inhalers are not sufficient treatment for anaphylaxis

Patients must understand that antihistamines and inhaled beta-agonists can treat some symptoms of allergic reactions (urticaria, pruritus, and bronchospasm, respectively), but they cannot reverse laryngeal edema or hypotension and are too slow acting to be effective in rapidly developing anaphylaxis (table 1) [1,2].

Antihistamines and asthma inhalers alone may appear to adequately control symptoms in anaphylaxis in some instances, but it is unclear if improvement is due to the medications or the patient's own corrective physiologic responses. Therefore, clinicians and patients must regard epinephrine as the first and best treatment for anaphylaxis.
When to use it
Clinicians should use plain language to explain to patients when to self-administer epinephrine. In the setting of an allergic reaction, patients should use epinephrine immediately if they:
● Are having trouble breathing
● Feel tightness in the throat
● Feel lightheaded or think they might pass out

Symptom and circumstance-based reasons to administer epinephrine (see 'Instructing patients when to self-administer epinephrine' below) suggest using the life-saving medication in circumstances that may not technically be considered anaphylaxis. For example, to administer epinephrine when the individual:
● Has food allergies and is vomiting repeatedly shortly after eating
● Is coughing repeatedly during an allergic reaction (indicating bronchospasm)
● Had previous anaphylaxis and develops widespread hives after a suspected or known ingestion of the allergen
● Has definitely eaten a trigger food that previously caused severe anaphylaxis and is having any symptoms [3,41]

In a Delphi panel assessment of expert opinion, there was 91 percent agreement that there should be no difference in decision-making to administer nasal versus injected epinephrine in the community [42].
How to use autoinjectors and nasal epinephrine

Epinephrine should ideally be injected into the mid-outer part of the thigh, into the underlying muscle. Intramuscular (IM) injection is preferable to subcutaneous injection as it results in more rapid systemic absorption [31,37]. Patients should be instructed to hold the device with a closed fist (ie, like a baton, with thumb/fingers away from either end) as accidental injection of the thumb/fingers or palm can occur if the autoinjector is inverted [43]. Children may not hold still for an injection, and caregivers should hold the child's leg firmly in place. This may require that a small child be placed on the ground. A second caregiver can secure the child's body, or a lone caregiver can immobilize the child's body with their own in order to leave two hands free, one to hold the thigh and the other to hold the autoinjector. The autoinjector should be held in place for at least three seconds after the injection. Instructions for different devices suggest 3 to 10 seconds, although most of the medicine is released from the device within the first second [44].

For nasal epinephrine, it should be noted that the device is used in a different manner than typical nasal sprays in that the device is not to be primed, is placed fully into the nostril without angling, and is not sniffed after activation. We suggest that adults supervise or administer nasal epinephrine for children experiencing anaphylaxis, as appropriate, to ensure adequate administration.

Patients should be instructed to stay with other people if possible during an allergic reaction. There is no need to undress before using the autoinjector as the needles are designed to penetrate clothing. However, we typically instruct patients to raise skirts or lower pants, if possible, to avoid an obstruction such as a buckle or contents of a pocket.

The clinician should demonstrate how to use the specific autoinjector that is being prescribed by using the specific training device for that autoinjector. Detailed written instructions are provided separately (see 'Information for patients' below). Manufacturers also provide DVDs and videos on their websites.
Use it without delay
Patients should understand that epinephrine is most effective when given within the first few minutes of an allergic reaction.
Call for help and go to the emergency department

If the patient is alone, epinephrine should be self-administered first, and then the patient should call for help and possibly be transported to the nearest emergency department (ED) in case the symptoms of anaphylaxis worsen or recur without further exposure to the trigger. It is important to make clear to patients that the reason for activating emergency medical services (EMS; 911 in Canada and the United States) and proceeding to the ED is the possibility of worsening or recurrent symptoms. Some patients misinterpret instructions to go to the ED as evidence that epinephrine is dangerous and that they must be examined whenever they have self-administered it, which is not the case. This, in turn, can cause them to avoid use.

Most reactions respond to one dose of epinephrine and do not require additional treatment. However, a decision not to proceed to an ED could also carry serious risks should the symptoms worsen and require additional interventions. The 2023 anaphylaxis practice parameter suggested that patients be counseled that immediate activation of emergency medical services may not be required if there is prompt, complete, and durable response to the treatment with self-administered epinephrine if additional epinephrine and medical care are readily available should they be needed [3]. An international consensus report identified multiple circumstances to activate EMS, including the individual being alone; receiving more than one dose of epinephrine; not having additional doses available; being >30 minutes from a hospital; having severe cardiovascular, neurologic, or respiratory symptoms before the first dose; or having continued mild, moderate, or severe cardiovascular, neurologic, or respiratory symptoms after the first dose [45].

Provider advice regarding home management should be individualized, and we favor having the patient proceed to an ED in most situations. It may be reasonable to have home management under circumstances such as close proximity to an ED, confidence in patient self-assessments, prompt and excellent response to treatment, access to additional autoinjectors and comfort with use, and patient circumstances (such as past reactions being mild/self-limited, not having significant asthma, etc). Circumstances that would argue against home management include any reluctance to treat, lack of additional epinephrine doses, patient not being comfortable, past serious reactions, incomplete response to treatment, etc. These considerations are not an exhaustive list, and ultimately such decisions would need to be made in communication with a health care provider.
Even if the ED is in close proximity or emergency medical services are en route, epinephrine should still be administered.

If patients become lightheaded, they should lie down with their legs elevated, if possible, in order to increase blood flow to vital organs. Similarly, if the patient loses consciousness in the caregiver's presence, the patient should be placed on their back with legs elevated.

Patients should never be propped up during anaphylaxis. Rising to an upright position during severe anaphylaxis has been associated with sudden death due to the "empty ventricle syndrome" [46]. Patients should be transported to an emergency medical facility in the supine position.
More than one dose may be needed
Patients should be advised that a second dose may be needed if symptoms do not appear to be stabilizing or improving in five minutes or are getting worse [3,37].
Practice with the training device

Autoinjectors are dispensed with a training device that is identical to the autoinjector but does not contain a needle or medication. Patients/caregivers should practice periodically with a training device. They should also use the trainer to teach others who may need to administer the epinephrine if the patient is incapacitated. They should also be warned that the actual/live autoinjector device may have more recoil than the trainer and that they should be prepared for this and continue to hold the device firmly against the thigh [47].
Teach others

Patients should be encouraged to inform and educate appropriate friends, caretakers, colleagues, and food providers about their allergic condition. It may be essential that those around them are able to recognize an allergic reaction and react effectively, both by administering epinephrine and calling for assistance if the patient is incapacitated.
Patients and caregivers should use the training devices to teach others how to administer epinephrine. (See "Food allergy in schools and camps".)
Replace the devices prior to expiration

Devices for self-administration of epinephrine have a limited shelf life and should be replaced prior to expiration. The labeled shelf life of autoinjectable epinephrine is 12 to 15 months. Thus, some patients renew their autoinjectable epinephrine prescription on their birthday or at the start of the school or calendar year to link renewal to an annual event. Nasal spray epinephrine has a longer labeled shelf life of 24 months for the 1 mg dose and 30 months for the 2 mg dose.

Autoinjectors have a window to inspect for discoloration of the solution or precipitated material in the solution, which are signs that the solution is losing potency. However, ideally, expired autoinjectors should also be replaced, even if the solution remains clear.
Use of expired devices
Patients should be informed that it is preferable to use an out-of-date device rather than not administering epinephrine at all [48].
At least three studies have found that expired autoinjectors retain significant potency, even up to four years after the expiration date:
● One study found that autoinjector epinephrine solutions that were within 24 months of their expiration dates still contained at least 90 percent of the labeled dose [49].

● Another study found that, among 31 expired autoinjectors, those less than 12 months past expiration contained 88 to 100 percent of the intended dose, and the oldest (50 months past expiration) contained 84 to 88 percent of the intended dose [50].

● Another study that measured the active enantiomer found that 65 percent of autoinjector devices retained >90 percent of activity over almost two years [51]. The 0.3 mg devices maintained potency better than the 0.15 mg devices: Within 36 months post-expiration, 93 percent of adult devices and 66 percent of pediatric devices retained >90 percent potency.
One study of the nasal spray epinephrine device found that potency remained within 96.6 to 97.9 at 30 months for the 2 mg dose and 92.5 to 94 percent at 24 months for the 1 mg dose [52].
Storage

Patients should be instructed to keep epinephrine devices in locations with neutral temperatures (waist pack, purse, cabinets) rather than locations where the unit may overheat or freeze (glove compartment of a car, in an uninsulated bag on the beach). The devices should not be refrigerated.

● For the autoinjectable devices, freezing and thawing appear to have less effect on epinephrine potency than storage at excessively hot temperatures [53-55]. A study examined the effects of storage of nine EpiPens for 12 hours in various locations inside a car on a summer day and found that temperatures within the car reached as high as 62°C (143°F; highest in the glove compartment) and that this single exposure resulted in decrements of 3 to 14 percent in the concentration of epinephrine, without changes in the appearance of the solution [56]. In another study, the syringe-based autoinjectable epinephrine retained more than 90 percent potency over six months at high heat (40°C, 104°F), whereas epinephrine in the cartridge-based device fell below specification to 79.6 percent [52]. Epinephrine in both types of devices had significant potency loss at more extreme heat (50°C, 122°F) over three months.

● The nasal spray device maintained adequate potency after five freeze-thaw cycles over 14 days, six months at high heat (40°C, 104°F), and three months at extreme heat (50°C, 122°F) [52]. The product insert for the nasal spray epinephrine device indicates that exposure to high temperatures up to 122°F is allowed for a few days.
Based on limited data and information from the US Food and Drug Administration, autoinjectors are unlikely to be adversely affected by radiograph equipment at airport security [57,58].
AREAS OF UNCERTAINTY FOR THE PRESCRIBING CLINICIAN
There are several areas of uncertainty for prescribing epinephrine and teaching patients about when it is appropriate to give the medication. These situations require clinical judgment.
Oral allergy syndrome

The risk of a systemic reaction in a patient with oral allergy syndrome and the relative indications for prescription of an epinephrine device are reviewed separately. (See "Pollen-food allergy syndrome (oral allergy syndrome): Management and prognosis", section on 'Indications for epinephrine'.)
Other scenarios
There may be less obvious circumstances where prescribing epinephrine is also appropriate [2,59]:
● It may be unclear from the clinical history whether anaphylaxis occurred, and clinical judgment may be needed to decide whether it did occur.

● An individual may have experienced a mild reaction to an allergen that is known to cause severe reactions (eg, a peanut/tree nut allergy). As an example, it would be reasonable to prescribe epinephrine for a child with severe eczema who was found to have peanut allergy and placed on a peanut-free diet but who had displayed only flares of eczema after eating peanut and never had a more serious reaction. Such patients may be at risk for anaphylaxis if subsequently exposed to the culprit allergen [60].
● An individual may have had an allergic reaction with clinical features that may indicate a higher risk of anaphylaxis on a future exposure, such as reactions to trace amounts of a food.
● There may be comorbid diseases or medications that increase the risk for a severe reaction, such as asthma or the use of beta blockers.
Instructing patients when to self-administer epinephrine

Certain symptom combinations, particularly with known or likely exposure to an allergen, are indications to inject epinephrine, as reviewed above [41]. Infants may display unique symptoms during anaphylaxis that should be reviewed accordingly [61]. (See "Anaphylaxis in infants".)
There are circumstances where it may be appropriate to instruct patients to self-administer even though serious symptoms have not occurred:
● If symptoms are mild but the patient is in a remote location.
● If the symptoms are mild but the reaction appears to be progressing rapidly.
● If the patient or caregiver is uncertain about the severity of the reaction, in which case it is preferable to administer epinephrine rather than withhold it.
● If there has been a known ingestion of a food or an insect sting that previously caused a severe reaction and any symptoms develop.
Knowledge about the nature of the exposure is also helpful in deciding whether to administer epinephrine.

● For example, if it is known that a food allergen was rubbed into the eye but definitely not ingested, then progression to anaphylaxis is unlikely and symptoms such as eyelid angioedema would not be a reason to give epinephrine. However, if the allergen was definitely ingested, the victim had a history of severe anaphylaxis to the same trigger, and eyelid angioedema was noted, it would be reasonable to give epinephrine.

● A child with asthma and an upper respiratory infection who ate a presumably safe meal and then exercised and developed severe wheezing is not likely experiencing anaphylaxis but rather an asthma exacerbation and would warrant inhaled bronchodilator therapy. In contrast, a child with severe asthma and peanut allergy who ate a peanut cookie and developed severe wheezing would warrant treatment with epinephrine.
Responsibilities of older children and adolescents

As children at risk for anaphylaxis mature, they need to become responsible for recognizing and treating anaphylaxis. In an online survey of 88 pediatric allergists, participants were asked about the age at which children are able to begin assuming these responsibilities [62]. These allergists most frequently responded that children aged 9 to 11 years should be able to describe some symptoms of anaphylaxis, recognize the need for epinephrine, and demonstrate correct use of an autoinjector. By age 12 to 14 years, most allergists expected children to take some responsibility for self-administering epinephrine when needed. They individualized the timing based on assessment of patient readiness factors, including medical history, developmental level, and ability to demonstrate correct autoinjector technique. It is important to note that a similar survey of parents and caregivers indicated that these individuals perceived the transition period as roughly three years earlier than the allergists, indicating the need to discuss whether children are capable of taking on these responsibilities on an individual basis [63].
PRINTABLE ACTION PLANS
Printable action plans are available from multiple sources:

● The American Academy of Allergy, Asthma, and Immunology has devised an "Anaphylaxis Emergency Action Plan" (available in English and Spanish) that can be personalized and provided to any patient who has experienced anaphylaxis. This plan provides clear instructions for patients about how to treat an anaphylaxis episode and gives both the clinician and the patient an opportunity to personalize the instructions.
● Action plans specific to children are also available from the American Academy of Pediatrics (Allergy and Anaphylaxis Emergency Plan, available in English and Spanish).
● Versions of action plans designed specifically for patients with food allergy are available from the Food Allergy Research and Education (FARE) website.

● The Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America offers action plans for children under age three years and for ages three years and up in multiple languages that include instructions about whether to activate emergency medical services [64].
SOCIETY GUIDELINE LINKS
Links to society and government-sponsored guidelines from selected countries and regions around the world are provided separately. (See "Society guideline links: Anaphylaxis".)
INFORMATION FOR PATIENTS

UpToDate offers two types of patient education materials, "The Basics" and "Beyond the Basics." The Basics patient education pieces are written in plain language, at the 5th to 6th grade reading level, and they answer the four or five key questions a patient might have about a given condition. These articles are best for patients who want a general overview and who prefer short, easy-to-read materials. Beyond the Basics patient education pieces are longer, more sophisticated, and more detailed. These articles are written at the 10th to 12th grade reading level and are best for patients who want in-depth information and are comfortable with some medical jargon.

Here are the patient education articles that are relevant to this topic. We encourage you to print or email these topics to your patients. (You can also locate patient education articles on a variety of subjects by searching on "patient education" and the keyword(s) of interest.)
● Basics topic (see "Patient education: How to give epinephrine (The Basics)")
● Beyond the Basics topic (see "Patient education: Using epinephrine for anaphylaxis self-treatment (Beyond the Basics)")

For patients with diagnosed anaphylaxis, three key steps include prescription of epinephrine, patient education, and follow-up evaluation [37]. Epinephrine should always be prescribed in the context of a comprehensive care plan, including instructions on allergen avoidance, as well as indications for injection of epinephrine and instructions on activating additional emergency services (eg, calling 911).
SUMMARY AND RECOMMENDATIONS

● Duties of clinician – When prescribing epinephrine autoinjectors for anaphylaxis self-treatment, clinicians must also provide patient-specific advice about when and how to administer epinephrine and dispel fears about its adverse effects. (See 'Introduction' above.)
● Pharmacology of epinephrine – Epinephrine is a sympathomimetic agent with multiple actions that can reverse the symptoms of anaphylaxis (table 1). (See 'Pharmacology' above.)

● Safety – Epinephrine will cause transient and minor adverse effects in most patients, even when used properly. However, patients should be reassured that serious adverse effects, such as myocardial ischemia, are rare with the doses delivered by an autoinjector or nasal spray. Furthermore, untreated anaphylaxis itself is associated with myocardial ischemia and dysrhythmias. Thus, all patients with past anaphylaxis should have access to epinephrine for self-treatment. (See 'Adverse effects' above.)

● Available devices – Several different autoinjector devices and a nasal spray are available, which vary in ease of use and cost. Prefilled, sealed syringes containing epinephrine are another option that is more commonly used in resource-limited settings. Once a device is selected, we suggest designating the specific name and description of the product on the prescription order and providing patient education that is specific to that product. (See 'Available devices and training' above.)

● Dosing of nasal spray – The doses of the available nasal spray are 2 mg for children and adults weighing ≥30 kg (66 lb) and 1 mg for children weighing 15 kg (33 lb) to <30 kg. (See 'Nasal spray' above.)

● Dosing of autoinjectors – Most epinephrine autoinjectors are available in doses of 0.15 mg and 0.3 mg. One manufacturer produces a device for infants that contains 0.1 mg (table 2 and table 3). The manufacturer's labeled dosing ranges differ from some expert opinions reflected here.
• The 0.3 mg dose is appropriate for children and adults weighing 25 kg or more (55 lb or more). Individuals who are overweight or obese should have access to multiple doses. (See 'Dosing' above.)

• Dosing in young children and infants is more difficult as the available doses result in doses either below or above the ideal dose for many. The 0.15 mg dose may be used for children between 10 and up to 25 kg (22 to <55 lb) if the 0.1 mg dose is not available. If the 0.1 mg autoinjector is available, the switch to the 0.15 mg dose could be at 13 kg (28.6 lb). (See 'Children' above.)

• For infants and small children weighing 7.5 kg (16.5 lb) to <13 kg (<28.6 lb), the 0.1 mg dose is ideal, but the 0.15 mg dose can be prescribed if the 0.1 mg dose is unavailable. (See 'Small children' above.)

● Teaching points – There are several important teaching points that should be emphasized when instructing patients in optimal use of epinephrine, which address most patients' areas of concern and confusion. This information should be reviewed with patients at regular intervals. (See 'Key teaching points' above.)

● Issues requiring clinical judgment – Clinical situations arise in which it is not clear if epinephrine should be administered. As an example, it is reasonable to instruct a patient with severe anaphylaxis to food who subsequently had a known ingestion of the culprit food to self-administer epinephrine even before any symptoms have developed. (See 'Areas of uncertainty for the prescribing clinician' above.)

articles.plain_text:
INTRODUCTION

Epinephrine is the drug of choice in the treatment of anaphylaxis, and prompt first-aid management requires the patient at risk for anaphylaxis to carry self-administered epinephrine [1-3]. An epinephrine autoinjector is the most common form of self-administered epinephrine available worldwide, with a nasal administration device also US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved. When prescribing these devices, clinicians must teach patients how and when to use them and dispel fears about adverse effects. Epinephrine carried for self-administration may be lifesaving for patients but only if patients are willing and able to use these devices effectively.

PHARMACOLOGY

Epinephrine is a sympathomimetic agent with multiple actions that can reverse the symptoms of anaphylaxis. (See "Anaphylaxis: Emergency treatment".)

Beneficial effects

Epinephrine acts as an agonist at alpha-1 receptors to mediate increased vasoconstriction, increased peripheral vascular resistance, and decreased mucosal edema. Agonist effects at beta-2 receptors result in bronchodilation and decreased mediator release from mast cells and basophils (table 1) [4].

Adverse effects

Even when administered properly, epinephrine is often associated with minor and transient adverse effects such as tremor, dizziness, palpitations, anxiety, restlessness, and headache (table 1) [4].

In contrast, serious adverse effects such as myocardial ischemia are rare after injection of a 0.3 mg dose in an adult or a 0.15 mg dose in a child. Such effects occur more commonly with epinephrine overdose, especially after intravenous administration. Reluctance to administer epinephrine due to fear of adverse cardiac effects should be countered by the awareness that myocardial ischemia and dysrhythmias can also occur in children and adults with anaphylaxis who have not received epinephrine treatment and in whom no cardiovascular disease can be found after the episode [5,6].

Unintentional injections and other injuries

The rate of unintentional injections of epinephrine from autoinjectors is high [7,8], with more than 15,000 such events being reported voluntarily to the American Association of Poison Control Centers from 1994 to 2007 and 6806 in 2013 to 2014, mostly involving injection into the digit or thumb [7,8]. In a retrospective series of 365 unintentional injections specifically to the hand, all patients had complete resolution of symptoms without the need for admission or surgery [9]. In this series, warm water soaks alone were used in 32 percent, and no drug therapy was administered in 77 percent. In 23 percent, various vasodilatory therapies were given (including topical nitroglycerin paste or local injection[s] of phentolamine). Most patients had resolution of symptoms within two hours. A systematic review found phentolamine to be the most effective treatment [10]. Patients should practice with a trainer and understand that, for pen-type devices, they should use a closed fist (like a baton) with thumb over their fingers to avoid injecting into a digit.

Other injuries related to use of epinephrine autoinjectors include lacerations, embedded needles, and injection-site infections (Clostridium perfringens) [11]. Full or partial injection into a blood vessel may occur, potentially resulting in high systolic blood pressure [12].

Contraindications

There are no absolute contraindications to the administration of epinephrine for anaphylaxis [1-3]. Therefore, all patients who have experienced anaphylaxis should have access to epinephrine for self-treatment, including pregnant patients at risk and patients who may be at greater risk for serious adverse effects, such as older individuals with cardiovascular disease. This includes patients who are sensitive to sulfite preservatives, which are present in all epinephrine devices. (See "Allergic and asthmatic reactions to food additives", section on 'Sulfites'.)

AVAILABLE DEVICES AND TRAINING

Choice of device

The choice of device is heavily influenced by patient values and preferences as well as the availability of the various options. Patient-important factors may include cost/insurance coverage, fear of needles/pain with injectable forms, frequency of device replacement, and stability of the drug at more extreme temperatures (eg, a landscaper who works in a hot climate or a ski instructor in the winter). A study using a commercial insurance database from 2015 to 2019 in the United States found that, with the advent of generic devices, 61 percent of patients paid $20 or less for a generic autoinjector, although 7.6 percent still paid over $200 [13].

Autoinjectors

The following preloaded epinephrine autoinjectors are available in the United States:

● EpiPen (brand name) – Containing 0.3 mg per dose

● EpiPen Jr (brand name) – Containing 0.15 mg per dose

● Authorized generics of EpiPen – Containing 0.3 or 0.15 mg per dose

● Authorized generics of Adrenaclick – Containing 0.3 or 0.15 mg per dose (brand name no longer available)

● Auvi-Q (brand name; Allerject [brand name] in Canada) – Containing 0.3 mg, 0.15 mg, or 0.1 mg per dose (provides audible directions to guide user)

In Canada (and Europe, among others), another device, the Emerade autoinjector, is available as 0.15 mg, 0.3 mg, and 0.5 mg. Other branded and generic autoinjectors are available in other countries.

Differences in the design and use of epinephrine self-injection products available need to be considered in the context of patient skills and preferences [14].

Nasal spray

An epinephrine nasal spray (neffy [brand name]) containing a single dose of 2 mg that is sprayed into one nostril is approved for use in children and adults weighing ≥30 kg (66 lb), and a 1 mg epinephrine nasal spray is approved for the use in children 15 kg (33 lb) to <30 kg [15]. If symptoms do not improve, a second device can be used to administer a second dose to the same nostril, starting five minutes after the first dose. Studies have been conducted with active upper respiratory tract symptoms and with nasal allergen challenge to suggest sufficient epinephrine exposure in these conditions [16,17]. In one of these, an open-label, randomized crossover study of 43 adults with seasonal allergic rhinitis undergoing nasal challenge, it was confirmed that use of the same nostril for the second dose resulted in improved pharmacokinetics (ie, sustained epinephrine exposure) compared with use of the contralateral nostril or intramuscular (IM) injection, consistent with the manufacturer's recommendations [17]. There is still a concern that the nasal spray may not be absorbed as intended in patients with conditions that alter the integrity of nasal mucosa, such as nasal polyposis or past nasal surgery, conditions that have not been studied, and patients with these conditions may be better served by an autoinjector.

Approval was based on studies of patients not experiencing anaphylaxis, in which this intranasal dose resulted in similar blood levels as those obtained with IM epinephrine given by syringe or autoinjectors [18-21]. However, a subsequent study of 15 children experiencing anaphylaxis during oral food challenges found that epinephrine nasal spray successfully treated symptoms, and no patient needed a second dose to treat the acute reactions [22].

Prefilled syringes

The provision of a syringe prefilled with epinephrine, stored away from light and kept for a brief period, such as three months, is a low-cost alternative but suffers from concerns about sterility and stability [23,24]. This option may be more suited to resource-limited regions. A prefilled syringe (Symjepi [brand name]) containing 0.15 mg or 0.3 mg of epinephrine per dose was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) but is now out of manufacture.

Self-filled syringe

The prescription of ampules of epinephrine and a syringe as a low-cost alternative has been discussed, but this approach suffers from potential dosing errors when used by laypersons in an emergency [25]. Thus, this option should be reserved for patients who do not have an alternative form of administration available.

Training

We suggest designating the specific name and description of the product intended to be dispensed on the prescription order and providing patient education that is specific to that product. Training devices that do not contain needles or epinephrine are available to clinicians and patients from the manufacturers in most cases and are sometimes dispensed at the pharmacy when the patient fills the prescription. In addition, manufacturers provide detailed instructions and videos online. Studies suggest that recurrent training may be required to use autoinjectors optimally [26].

Number of doses to dispense

There are no global consensus guidelines about how many doses should be dispensed for each patient [2,3]. Decision-making regarding prescribing one or more devices might include past reaction history (such as biphasic anaphylaxis and past reactions requiring more than one dose), risk of severe anaphylaxis, access to additional care, and other factors. Many allergy specialists prescribe at least two for all patients, and some prescribe more. The following should be considered:

● A systematic review and meta-analysis that included 86 studies found that 7.7 percent of anaphylaxis cases from any cause were treated with more than one dose of epinephrine. Considering epinephrine-treated reactions where the subsequent doses were administered by heath care professionals, the rate was 11 percent for food allergy and 17 percent for venom allergy [27].

● There is a theoretical concern that teenagers and adults who are overweight or obese may be underdosed (on a per kg basis) when treated with the 0.3 mg autoinjector, although this has not been proven [4,28].

● The distance between the patient's home/work/school and the nearest medical facility also impacts the number of doses that should be available to the patient.

● Concerns about overprescribing additional units and generating excessive cost have been raised [29]. As an example, having multiple units available at school for each at-risk child when many units are already available in the school for other children may not be necessary [30].

DOSING

Adults

Autoinjectors with 0.3 mg of epinephrine per dose and the nasal spray (which contains 2 mg) are appropriate for adults.

Adults with obesity

Adults who are overweight or obese should have access to at least two doses of epinephrine.

In patients with significant adipose tissue on the anterolateral thigh, the needle of an epinephrine autoinjector may not be of sufficient length to reach the underlying muscle, and compression of the tissue during injection is minimal. Compared with subcutaneous injection, intramuscular (IM) injection of epinephrine results in higher and more rapid plasma concentrations and is therefore the recommended route of delivery [31]. However, in a series of 28 patients, needle length was not sufficient to reach the underlying muscle of the anterolateral thigh in 68 percent of patients [32]. The issue was more common in females, even those with normal body mass index (BMI). These findings may raise concerns about suboptimal delivery, although human treatment studies have not been undertaken to quantify the potential differences in serum dose and kinetics. In addition, a retrospective chart review of emergency department patients with anaphylaxis, mostly children, found that the need for a second dose did not correlate with overweight status, suggesting repeat dosing is not a result of obesity or suboptimal medication delivery [28]. Having a second autoinjector available addresses the concern that treatment may be inadequate for this or other reasons, pending further study of the implications of needle length and patient weight. Use of the nasal spray may be appropriate if obesity is a particular concern.

Children

In most countries, epinephrine autoinjectors are available in only two fixed doses: 0.15 mg and 0.3 mg. One manufacturer has a 0.1 mg dose (Auvi-Q [brand name]). The availability of specific doses in autoinjectable form presents difficulties in delivering an appropriate dose to many children. The recommended dose of epinephrine for children is 0.01 mg/kg, up to 0.3 mg. Therefore, the premeasured autoinjectors technically contain the recommended dose only for a 10 kg (22 lb), 15 kg (33 lb), or 30 kg (66 lb) individual. The nasal spray containing 1 mg epinephrine is appropriate for children weighing 15 to <30 kg.

Small children

The prescribing information for autoinjectors containing 0.15 mg of epinephrine indicates that the dose is intended for patients weighing 15 to 30 kg (33 to 66 lb). Using these manufacturers' guidelines, children weighing 25 kg (55 lb) would receive the 0.15 mg dose, although the optimal dose for a child of that weight is higher (0.25 mg). Furthermore, little information is provided about dosing in a child weighing less than 15 kg (33 lb), other than the caveat that dosing decisions are the responsibility of the prescribing clinician.

Examples of dosing issues raised by fixed-dose autoinjectors in infants and small children include the following:

● For a 7.5 kg (16.5 lb) child – The 0.1 mg autoinjector delivers 133 percent of the ideal dose, and the 0.15 mg autoinjector delivers 200 percent of the ideal dose.

● For a 10 kg (22 lb) child – The 0.15 mg autoinjector delivers 150 percent of the ideal dose.

● For a 12.5 kg (27.5 lb) child – The 0.1 mg dose delivers only 80 percent of the ideal dose, while the 0.15 mg autoinjector delivers 120 percent of the ideal dose.

● For a 20 kg (44 lb) child – The 0.15 mg autoinjector delivers only 75 percent of the ideal dose, while the 0.3 mg autoinjector delivers 150 percent of the ideal dose.

● For a 25 kg (55 lb) child – The 0.15 mg autoinjector delivers only 60 percent of the ideal dose, while the 0.3 mg autoinjector delivers 120 percent of the ideal dose.

Despite the lack of precision in dosing with autoinjectors, the alternative (ie, drawing up epinephrine in a syringe to obtain the correct weight-based dose) is associated with delayed administration, inaccurate dosing, and potential loss of the dose. A study of the ability of parents without medical training to utilize an ampule and syringe after receiving verbal and written instructions in a nonurgent setting found this method to be error prone and slow [25].

One study indicated that children generally tolerate higher doses of epinephrine without serious adverse events. In a randomized trial, children (aged four to eight years and weighing 15 to 30 kg [33 to 66 lb]) who were at risk for anaphylaxis received either 0.15 mg or 0.3 mg of epinephrine IM [33]. The higher dose resulted in significantly higher systolic blood pressures compared with the lower dose but was also associated with transient nausea, palpitations, and headache.

Suggested approach

To provide additional guidance to the clinician, a clinical report from the American Academy of Pediatrics reviewed the risks and benefits of selecting the 0.15 mg or the 0.3 mg fixed doses for children of different weights, and an Allergy and Anaphylaxis Emergency Plan is linked to this report, reflecting updated recommendations about dosing for the available epinephrine devices based on weight [34]. The report references European guidelines, suggesting the 0.15 mg autoinjector may be used for infants weighing as little as 7.5 kg (16.5 lb) [35]. Subsequent to this report, the 0.1 mg Auvi-Q (brand name) became available in some countries and is labeled for use in infants and toddlers 7.5 to 15 kg (16.5 to 33 lb). The following summarizes our suggested approach based on these guidelines and a 2023 practice parameter [3], but specific decisions should be individualized according to patient characteristics and caretaker preferences (eg, severity of allergy, comorbid conditions, cost/availability of autoinjectors, caretaker proficiency with using a syringe and ampule) (table 2 and table 3):

● Ideal dosing for infants under 7.5 kg (16.5 lb) would require an ampule and syringe or a prefilled syringe to deliver 0.01 mg/kg. The 0.1 mg autoinjector (only available as Auvi-Q [brand name]) could also be considered for infants near the upper end of this weight range if an autoinjector is believed to have important benefits over other delivery devices.

● For infants/children weighing 7.5 to less than 13 kg (16.5 to <28.6 lb), the clinician has the following prescribing option: Prescribe a 0.1 mg (ideal) or a 0.15 mg autoinjector (option if the 0.1 mg autoinjector is not accessible).

● Children weighing 13 kg (28.6 lb) to less than 25 kg (55 lb) can receive the 0.15 mg dose.

● Children weighing 25 kg or more (55 lb or more) can receive the 0.3 mg dose autoinjector.

● Dosing might be individualized for children with severe past reactions, to select the higher of the two fixed doses at lower weights.

● In Canada, where the 0.5 mg Emerade device is available, the manufacturer suggests using this for adults >60 kg, and a Canadian position statement suggested this be prescribed for those weighing 45 kg (99 lb) or more [36].

KEY TEACHING POINTS

There are several important teaching points that should be emphasized when instructing patients in optimal use of epinephrine autoinjectors. These should be reviewed with patients at regular intervals. Patient information that reiterates these teaching points is also available. (See 'Information for patients' below.)

Anaphylaxis is unpredictable

Patients should understand that anaphylaxis is highly unpredictable [37]. One exposure to an allergen may result in mild symptoms while the next causes a life-threatening reaction or vice versa for reasons that are not fully understood.

Epinephrine is the best treatment available

The patient should be assured that epinephrine is the most effective treatment available for anaphylaxis and that having self-administered epinephrine available will enable the patient to start treatment without delay [3]. Fatal anaphylaxis is associated with lack of availability of epinephrine or failure to administer epinephrine promptly [38-40]. This fact may be expressed to the patient as the following: "In most cases of anaphylaxis that prove fatal, the person who died either did not have epinephrine available or had it available but did not use it. Thus, by having epinephrine and knowing how to use it, the patient already has a significant advantage."

Carry epinephrine at all times

Epinephrine autoinjectors or nasal sprays must be carried at all times in order to be available when the drug is actually needed. Patients may make the mistake of having their epinephrine on hand only in the setting where they spend most time (ie, home, school, or work). However, they may be at particular risk for anaphylaxis when out of their normal routines (eg, during exercise, while dining out, attending celebrations and banquets, or traveling). Thus, patients should devise a way for epinephrine to be available at all times. This may mean storing devices in multiple locations or carrying a small bag containing the device and other essential items that is taken everywhere, without exception.

Antihistamines or asthma inhalers are not sufficient treatment for anaphylaxis

Patients must understand that antihistamines and inhaled beta-agonists can treat some symptoms of allergic reactions (urticaria, pruritus, and bronchospasm, respectively), but they cannot reverse laryngeal edema or hypotension and are too slow acting to be effective in rapidly developing anaphylaxis (table 1) [1,2].

Antihistamines and asthma inhalers alone may appear to adequately control symptoms in anaphylaxis in some instances, but it is unclear if improvement is due to the medications or the patient's own corrective physiologic responses. Therefore, clinicians and patients must regard epinephrine as the first and best treatment for anaphylaxis.

When to use it

Clinicians should use plain language to explain to patients when to self-administer epinephrine. In the setting of an allergic reaction, patients should use epinephrine immediately if they:

● Are having trouble breathing

● Feel tightness in the throat

● Feel lightheaded or think they might pass out

Symptom and circumstance-based reasons to administer epinephrine (see 'Instructing patients when to self-administer epinephrine' below) suggest using the life-saving medication in circumstances that may not technically be considered anaphylaxis. For example, to administer epinephrine when the individual:

● Has food allergies and is vomiting repeatedly shortly after eating

● Is coughing repeatedly during an allergic reaction (indicating bronchospasm)

● Had previous anaphylaxis and develops widespread hives after a suspected or known ingestion of the allergen

● Has definitely eaten a trigger food that previously caused severe anaphylaxis and is having any symptoms [3,41]

In a Delphi panel assessment of expert opinion, there was 91 percent agreement that there should be no difference in decision-making to administer nasal versus injected epinephrine in the community [42].

How to use autoinjectors and nasal epinephrine

Epinephrine should ideally be injected into the mid-outer part of the thigh, into the underlying muscle. Intramuscular (IM) injection is preferable to subcutaneous injection as it results in more rapid systemic absorption [31,37]. Patients should be instructed to hold the device with a closed fist (ie, like a baton, with thumb/fingers away from either end) as accidental injection of the thumb/fingers or palm can occur if the autoinjector is inverted [43]. Children may not hold still for an injection, and caregivers should hold the child's leg firmly in place. This may require that a small child be placed on the ground. A second caregiver can secure the child's body, or a lone caregiver can immobilize the child's body with their own in order to leave two hands free, one to hold the thigh and the other to hold the autoinjector. The autoinjector should be held in place for at least three seconds after the injection. Instructions for different devices suggest 3 to 10 seconds, although most of the medicine is released from the device within the first second [44].

For nasal epinephrine, it should be noted that the device is used in a different manner than typical nasal sprays in that the device is not to be primed, is placed fully into the nostril without angling, and is not sniffed after activation. We suggest that adults supervise or administer nasal epinephrine for children experiencing anaphylaxis, as appropriate, to ensure adequate administration.

Patients should be instructed to stay with other people if possible during an allergic reaction. There is no need to undress before using the autoinjector as the needles are designed to penetrate clothing. However, we typically instruct patients to raise skirts or lower pants, if possible, to avoid an obstruction such as a buckle or contents of a pocket.

The clinician should demonstrate how to use the specific autoinjector that is being prescribed by using the specific training device for that autoinjector. Detailed written instructions are provided separately (see 'Information for patients' below). Manufacturers also provide DVDs and videos on their websites.

Use it without delay

Patients should understand that epinephrine is most effective when given within the first few minutes of an allergic reaction.

Call for help and go to the emergency department

If the patient is alone, epinephrine should be self-administered first, and then the patient should call for help and possibly be transported to the nearest emergency department (ED) in case the symptoms of anaphylaxis worsen or recur without further exposure to the trigger. It is important to make clear to patients that the reason for activating emergency medical services (EMS; 911 in Canada and the United States) and proceeding to the ED is the possibility of worsening or recurrent symptoms. Some patients misinterpret instructions to go to the ED as evidence that epinephrine is dangerous and that they must be examined whenever they have self-administered it, which is not the case. This, in turn, can cause them to avoid use.

Most reactions respond to one dose of epinephrine and do not require additional treatment. However, a decision not to proceed to an ED could also carry serious risks should the symptoms worsen and require additional interventions. The 2023 anaphylaxis practice parameter suggested that patients be counseled that immediate activation of emergency medical services may not be required if there is prompt, complete, and durable response to the treatment with self-administered epinephrine if additional epinephrine and medical care are readily available should they be needed [3]. An international consensus report identified multiple circumstances to activate EMS, including the individual being alone; receiving more than one dose of epinephrine; not having additional doses available; being >30 minutes from a hospital; having severe cardiovascular, neurologic, or respiratory symptoms before the first dose; or having continued mild, moderate, or severe cardiovascular, neurologic, or respiratory symptoms after the first dose [45].

Provider advice regarding home management should be individualized, and we favor having the patient proceed to an ED in most situations. It may be reasonable to have home management under circumstances such as close proximity to an ED, confidence in patient self-assessments, prompt and excellent response to treatment, access to additional autoinjectors and comfort with use, and patient circumstances (such as past reactions being mild/self-limited, not having significant asthma, etc). Circumstances that would argue against home management include any reluctance to treat, lack of additional epinephrine doses, patient not being comfortable, past serious reactions, incomplete response to treatment, etc. These considerations are not an exhaustive list, and ultimately such decisions would need to be made in communication with a health care provider.

Even if the ED is in close proximity or emergency medical services are en route, epinephrine should still be administered.

If patients become lightheaded, they should lie down with their legs elevated, if possible, in order to increase blood flow to vital organs. Similarly, if the patient loses consciousness in the caregiver's presence, the patient should be placed on their back with legs elevated.

Patients should never be propped up during anaphylaxis. Rising to an upright position during severe anaphylaxis has been associated with sudden death due to the "empty ventricle syndrome" [46]. Patients should be transported to an emergency medical facility in the supine position.

More than one dose may be needed

Patients should be advised that a second dose may be needed if symptoms do not appear to be stabilizing or improving in five minutes or are getting worse [3,37].

Practice with the training device

Autoinjectors are dispensed with a training device that is identical to the autoinjector but does not contain a needle or medication. Patients/caregivers should practice periodically with a training device. They should also use the trainer to teach others who may need to administer the epinephrine if the patient is incapacitated. They should also be warned that the actual/live autoinjector device may have more recoil than the trainer and that they should be prepared for this and continue to hold the device firmly against the thigh [47].

Teach others

Patients should be encouraged to inform and educate appropriate friends, caretakers, colleagues, and food providers about their allergic condition. It may be essential that those around them are able to recognize an allergic reaction and react effectively, both by administering epinephrine and calling for assistance if the patient is incapacitated.

Patients and caregivers should use the training devices to teach others how to administer epinephrine. (See "Food allergy in schools and camps".)

Replace the devices prior to expiration

Devices for self-administration of epinephrine have a limited shelf life and should be replaced prior to expiration. The labeled shelf life of autoinjectable epinephrine is 12 to 15 months. Thus, some patients renew their autoinjectable epinephrine prescription on their birthday or at the start of the school or calendar year to link renewal to an annual event. Nasal spray epinephrine has a longer labeled shelf life of 24 months for the 1 mg dose and 30 months for the 2 mg dose.

Autoinjectors have a window to inspect for discoloration of the solution or precipitated material in the solution, which are signs that the solution is losing potency. However, ideally, expired autoinjectors should also be replaced, even if the solution remains clear.

Use of expired devices

Patients should be informed that it is preferable to use an out-of-date device rather than not administering epinephrine at all [48].

At least three studies have found that expired autoinjectors retain significant potency, even up to four years after the expiration date:

● One study found that autoinjector epinephrine solutions that were within 24 months of their expiration dates still contained at least 90 percent of the labeled dose [49].

● Another study found that, among 31 expired autoinjectors, those less than 12 months past expiration contained 88 to 100 percent of the intended dose, and the oldest (50 months past expiration) contained 84 to 88 percent of the intended dose [50].

● Another study that measured the active enantiomer found that 65 percent of autoinjector devices retained >90 percent of activity over almost two years [51]. The 0.3 mg devices maintained potency better than the 0.15 mg devices: Within 36 months post-expiration, 93 percent of adult devices and 66 percent of pediatric devices retained >90 percent potency.

One study of the nasal spray epinephrine device found that potency remained within 96.6 to 97.9 at 30 months for the 2 mg dose and 92.5 to 94 percent at 24 months for the 1 mg dose [52].

Storage

Patients should be instructed to keep epinephrine devices in locations with neutral temperatures (waist pack, purse, cabinets) rather than locations where the unit may overheat or freeze (glove compartment of a car, in an uninsulated bag on the beach). The devices should not be refrigerated.

● For the autoinjectable devices, freezing and thawing appear to have less effect on epinephrine potency than storage at excessively hot temperatures [53-55]. A study examined the effects of storage of nine EpiPens for 12 hours in various locations inside a car on a summer day and found that temperatures within the car reached as high as 62°C (143°F; highest in the glove compartment) and that this single exposure resulted in decrements of 3 to 14 percent in the concentration of epinephrine, without changes in the appearance of the solution [56]. In another study, the syringe-based autoinjectable epinephrine retained more than 90 percent potency over six months at high heat (40°C, 104°F), whereas epinephrine in the cartridge-based device fell below specification to 79.6 percent [52]. Epinephrine in both types of devices had significant potency loss at more extreme heat (50°C, 122°F) over three months.

● The nasal spray device maintained adequate potency after five freeze-thaw cycles over 14 days, six months at high heat (40°C, 104°F), and three months at extreme heat (50°C, 122°F) [52]. The product insert for the nasal spray epinephrine device indicates that exposure to high temperatures up to 122°F is allowed for a few days.

Based on limited data and information from the US Food and Drug Administration, autoinjectors are unlikely to be adversely affected by radiograph equipment at airport security [57,58].

AREAS OF UNCERTAINTY FOR THE PRESCRIBING CLINICIAN

There are several areas of uncertainty for prescribing epinephrine and teaching patients about when it is appropriate to give the medication. These situations require clinical judgment.

Oral allergy syndrome

The risk of a systemic reaction in a patient with oral allergy syndrome and the relative indications for prescription of an epinephrine device are reviewed separately. (See "Pollen-food allergy syndrome (oral allergy syndrome): Management and prognosis", section on 'Indications for epinephrine'.)

Other scenarios

There may be less obvious circumstances where prescribing epinephrine is also appropriate [2,59]:

● It may be unclear from the clinical history whether anaphylaxis occurred, and clinical judgment may be needed to decide whether it did occur.

● An individual may have experienced a mild reaction to an allergen that is known to cause severe reactions (eg, a peanut/tree nut allergy). As an example, it would be reasonable to prescribe epinephrine for a child with severe eczema who was found to have peanut allergy and placed on a peanut-free diet but who had displayed only flares of eczema after eating peanut and never had a more serious reaction. Such patients may be at risk for anaphylaxis if subsequently exposed to the culprit allergen [60].

● An individual may have had an allergic reaction with clinical features that may indicate a higher risk of anaphylaxis on a future exposure, such as reactions to trace amounts of a food.

● There may be comorbid diseases or medications that increase the risk for a severe reaction, such as asthma or the use of beta blockers.

Instructing patients when to self-administer epinephrine

Certain symptom combinations, particularly with known or likely exposure to an allergen, are indications to inject epinephrine, as reviewed above [41]. Infants may display unique symptoms during anaphylaxis that should be reviewed accordingly [61]. (See "Anaphylaxis in infants".)

There are circumstances where it may be appropriate to instruct patients to self-administer even though serious symptoms have not occurred:

● If symptoms are mild but the patient is in a remote location.

● If the symptoms are mild but the reaction appears to be progressing rapidly.

● If the patient or caregiver is uncertain about the severity of the reaction, in which case it is preferable to administer epinephrine rather than withhold it.

● If there has been a known ingestion of a food or an insect sting that previously caused a severe reaction and any symptoms develop.

Knowledge about the nature of the exposure is also helpful in deciding whether to administer epinephrine.

● For example, if it is known that a food allergen was rubbed into the eye but definitely not ingested, then progression to anaphylaxis is unlikely and symptoms such as eyelid angioedema would not be a reason to give epinephrine. However, if the allergen was definitely ingested, the victim had a history of severe anaphylaxis to the same trigger, and eyelid angioedema was noted, it would be reasonable to give epinephrine.

● A child with asthma and an upper respiratory infection who ate a presumably safe meal and then exercised and developed severe wheezing is not likely experiencing anaphylaxis but rather an asthma exacerbation and would warrant inhaled bronchodilator therapy. In contrast, a child with severe asthma and peanut allergy who ate a peanut cookie and developed severe wheezing would warrant treatment with epinephrine.

Responsibilities of older children and adolescents

As children at risk for anaphylaxis mature, they need to become responsible for recognizing and treating anaphylaxis. In an online survey of 88 pediatric allergists, participants were asked about the age at which children are able to begin assuming these responsibilities [62]. These allergists most frequently responded that children aged 9 to 11 years should be able to describe some symptoms of anaphylaxis, recognize the need for epinephrine, and demonstrate correct use of an autoinjector. By age 12 to 14 years, most allergists expected children to take some responsibility for self-administering epinephrine when needed. They individualized the timing based on assessment of patient readiness factors, including medical history, developmental level, and ability to demonstrate correct autoinjector technique. It is important to note that a similar survey of parents and caregivers indicated that these individuals perceived the transition period as roughly three years earlier than the allergists, indicating the need to discuss whether children are capable of taking on these responsibilities on an individual basis [63].

PRINTABLE ACTION PLANS

Printable action plans are available from multiple sources:

● The American Academy of Allergy, Asthma, and Immunology has devised an "Anaphylaxis Emergency Action Plan" (available in English and Spanish) that can be personalized and provided to any patient who has experienced anaphylaxis. This plan provides clear instructions for patients about how to treat an anaphylaxis episode and gives both the clinician and the patient an opportunity to personalize the instructions.

● Action plans specific to children are also available from the American Academy of Pediatrics (Allergy and Anaphylaxis Emergency Plan, available in English and Spanish).

● Versions of action plans designed specifically for patients with food allergy are available from the Food Allergy Research and Education (FARE) website.

● The Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America offers action plans for children under age three years and for ages three years and up in multiple languages that include instructions about whether to activate emergency medical services [64].

INFORMATION FOR PATIENTS

UpToDate offers two types of patient education materials, "The Basics" and "Beyond the Basics." The Basics patient education pieces are written in plain language, at the 5th to 6th grade reading level, and they answer the four or five key questions a patient might have about a given condition. These articles are best for patients who want a general overview and who prefer short, easy-to-read materials. Beyond the Basics patient education pieces are longer, more sophisticated, and more detailed. These articles are written at the 10th to 12th grade reading level and are best for patients who want in-depth information and are comfortable with some medical jargon.

Here are the patient education articles that are relevant to this topic. We encourage you to print or email these topics to your patients. (You can also locate patient education articles on a variety of subjects by searching on "patient education" and the keyword(s) of interest.)

● Basics topic (see "Patient education: How to give epinephrine (The Basics)")

● Beyond the Basics topic (see "Patient education: Using epinephrine for anaphylaxis self-treatment (Beyond the Basics)")

For patients with diagnosed anaphylaxis, three key steps include prescription of epinephrine, patient education, and follow-up evaluation [37]. Epinephrine should always be prescribed in the context of a comprehensive care plan, including instructions on allergen avoidance, as well as indications for injection of epinephrine and instructions on activating additional emergency services (eg, calling 911).

SUMMARY AND RECOMMENDATIONS

● Duties of clinician – When prescribing epinephrine autoinjectors for anaphylaxis self-treatment, clinicians must also provide patient-specific advice about when and how to administer epinephrine and dispel fears about its adverse effects. (See 'Introduction' above.)

● Pharmacology of epinephrine – Epinephrine is a sympathomimetic agent with multiple actions that can reverse the symptoms of anaphylaxis (table 1). (See 'Pharmacology' above.)

● Safety – Epinephrine will cause transient and minor adverse effects in most patients, even when used properly. However, patients should be reassured that serious adverse effects, such as myocardial ischemia, are rare with the doses delivered by an autoinjector or nasal spray. Furthermore, untreated anaphylaxis itself is associated with myocardial ischemia and dysrhythmias. Thus, all patients with past anaphylaxis should have access to epinephrine for self-treatment. (See 'Adverse effects' above.)

● Available devices – Several different autoinjector devices and a nasal spray are available, which vary in ease of use and cost. Prefilled, sealed syringes containing epinephrine are another option that is more commonly used in resource-limited settings. Once a device is selected, we suggest designating the specific name and description of the product on the prescription order and providing patient education that is specific to that product. (See 'Available devices and training' above.)

● Dosing of nasal spray – The doses of the available nasal spray are 2 mg for children and adults weighing ≥30 kg (66 lb) and 1 mg for children weighing 15 kg (33 lb) to <30 kg. (See 'Nasal spray' above.)

● Dosing of autoinjectors – Most epinephrine autoinjectors are available in doses of 0.15 mg and 0.3 mg. One manufacturer produces a device for infants that contains 0.1 mg (table 2 and table 3). The manufacturer's labeled dosing ranges differ from some expert opinions reflected here.

• The 0.3 mg dose is appropriate for children and adults weighing 25 kg or more (55 lb or more). Individuals who are overweight or obese should have access to multiple doses. (See 'Dosing' above.)

• Dosing in young children and infants is more difficult as the available doses result in doses either below or above the ideal dose for many. The 0.15 mg dose may be used for children between 10 and up to 25 kg (22 to <55 lb) if the 0.1 mg dose is not available. If the 0.1 mg autoinjector is available, the switch to the 0.15 mg dose could be at 13 kg (28.6 lb). (See 'Children' above.)

• For infants and small children weighing 7.5 kg (16.5 lb) to <13 kg (<28.6 lb), the 0.1 mg dose is ideal, but the 0.15 mg dose can be prescribed if the 0.1 mg dose is unavailable. (See 'Small children' above.)

● Teaching points – There are several important teaching points that should be emphasized when instructing patients in optimal use of epinephrine, which address most patients' areas of concern and confusion. This information should be reviewed with patients at regular intervals. (See 'Key teaching points' above.)

● Issues requiring clinical judgment – Clinical situations arise in which it is not clear if epinephrine should be administered. As an example, it is reasonable to instruct a patient with severe anaphylaxis to food who subsequently had a known ingestion of the culprit food to self-administer epinephrine even before any symptoms have developed. (See 'Areas of uncertainty for the prescribing clinician' above.)
